arm_instructions.map:
## Code navigation

- Start discovery with one scoped `slopdex map -g "<glob>" -i -e "<term|term>" -q "<short symbol concept>" --private --callers 2 --callees 2 <paths...>`. Immediately read plausible implementation ranges from the source files directly. Avoid mapping repeatedly, frontload the map in one call.

Required: one successful `slopdex map` before grep/read; other slopdex navigation is blocked.
Checkout and symbol vectors are ready; never override root/index/config.
For Go discovery add --ignore-errors -g '*.go' -g '!**/*_test.go'.

manifest.provenance_note: Historical job did not record slopdex source/binary identity; not eligible for automatic map reuse.

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Investigate how the checker handles an ordinary call to an overloaded generic function when an argument is a callback whose type depends on the selected overload. Identify three implementation functions: the one that obtains callable signatures from the callee's type and delegates typed calls; the one that coordinates candidate ordering, the successive type-relation passes, and failure reporting; and the one that evaluates individual candidates through arity checks, type-argument inference or validation, and contextual argument checking. Explain the flow between them, why a candidate may be checked again after initially excluding context-sensitive arguments, and what happens when no candidate succeeds. Base your explanation on this checkout's implementation; do not modify code.
tasks.title: Selecting an overload with context-sensitive arguments

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Trace how comparing a union-valued object's discriminant property with a literal changes the object's type inside the true and false branches. Identify three implementation functions: the one that computes a conditional flow node's type from its antecedent and the branch polarity; the one that handles discriminant-property comparisons, including any special handling of strict equality and inequality; and the fallback that narrows the accessed property and filters the original union's constituents. Explain their relationship, how the two branch polarities affect selection or exclusion of a member, and how optional property access and nullable types influence the fallback. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Recovering a union member from a branch condition

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Investigate Node-style resolution of a package whose export map includes a root entry, overlapping exact and wildcard subpaths, conditional targets, arrays of alternatives, and an explicitly blocked subpath. Identify three implementation functions: the one that interprets the package's export map for the requested root or subpath; the one that selects an exact or expanding subpath key and extracts the matched portion; and the recursive one that interprets the selected target and attempts resolution. Explain the flow between them, how wildcard precedence is determined, how conditions and arrays are traversed, and how an explicit null target differs from an unsuccessful alternative. Include where target paths are validated and where a matched target becomes a file lookup. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Resolving a package subpath through an export map

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. A project inherits several configurations from other directories, overrides some compiler options and file-selection settings, and encounters both source files and generated files with the same basename. Identify three implementation functions: the one that recursively combines the project's own configuration with its bases and adjusts inherited relative file specifications; the one that obtains an inherited configuration through the optional cache while accounting for the active resolution stack; and the one that expands validated file specifications into the final file list. Explain the flow across these stages, precedence among multiple bases and local settings, preservation of the origin of relative path mappings, circular-inheritance handling, and the different treatment of explicit files, wildcard matches, competing extensions, and JSON files. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: From layered configuration to the selected source files

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Trace how a program configured to use project-reference sources can follow a dependency whose expected declaration output has not been written to disk. Identify three implementation functions: the one that builds the referenced configuration's input-to-declaration-output and reverse associations; the filesystem helper that decides whether an expected declaration file can count as present based on its corresponding source; and the file-loading routine that checks project-reference redirection before reading and parsing the requested file. Explain how the associations support resolution and loading, where the source-versus-output policy enters the loading flow, how a redirected task is scheduled, and how an unmapped declaration path is distinguished from a mapped path whose source is missing. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Using a referenced project's sources before declaration output exists

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Investigate the incremental program-update path when an editor project knows that exactly one source file changed and the configuration object is unchanged. Identify three implementation functions: the project-level routine that attempts this optimization and manages ownership of parsed files; the compiler routine that tries replacing the changed file while retaining existing program data; and the predicate that compares the old and new file's structure-affecting metadata. Explain their flow, which import or reference changes invalidate the optimization, why some package redirects or synthetic imports require rebuilding even when the metadata predicate passes, and what happens to the speculatively acquired changed file and the references to unchanged parsed files on success versus fallback. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Deciding whether an editor edit permits program reuse

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Trace an auto-import completion for an identifier in an ordinary, non-content-mapped source file, from candidate selection to the client's later request for its details. Identify three implementation functions: the auto-import view routine that groups matching exports and chooses and orders their import fixes; the language-service resolve entry point that recovers the correct source file and checker from the completion item's stored data; and the details routine that handles the stored auto-import fix and attaches the resulting import edits. Explain how duplicate exports, alternative module spellings, JSX or type-only context, and fix ranking affect candidate selection, and how the lazy resolve path uses stored data rather than collecting auto-import candidates again. Include the special treatment of completions inside an import statement. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: From exported candidates to a resolved auto-import completion

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Investigate how the language service converts already-found symbol references into rename edits when a name participates in shorthand object properties, destructuring, or import and export aliases, and more than one reference may describe the same text range. Identify three implementation functions: the routine that validates the original node and builds workspace edits from the symbol-and-reference results; the helper that chooses replacement text according to the relationship between the renamed symbol and each occurrence; and the helper that consolidates edits by document and range. Explain their flow, why a shorthand or alias occurrence may require more than replacing the identifier, how edit construction handles occurrences that cannot be mapped back exactly to original text, and how identical duplicate edits differ from conflicting replacements at the same range. This is an implementation-understanding task; do not perform a rename or modify code.
tasks.title: Turning rename references into consistent workspace edits

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Trace the compiler transformation of a non-generator async function or async arrow when its parameter list contains defaults or rest parameters and its body depends on lexical bindings. Identify three implementation functions: the one that rewrites the outer parameter list; the one that constructs the lowered function body and manages forwarded arguments and captured bindings; and the visitor that rewrites individual await expressions. Explain how these stages fit together, how ordinary functions and arrows differ in parameter forwarding and function-length preservation, how lexical this and arguments are carried through the transformation, and why top-level await receives different treatment from await inside the function. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Preserving runtime semantics while lowering async functions

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Investigate how the parser decides whether angle-bracket tokens after an expression represent type arguments or should remain available for relational or shift-expression parsing. Identify three implementation functions: the one that attempts the type-argument parse and either commits or abandons it; the predicate that judges the tokens following the closing bracket; and the rollback routine that restores parser and scanner state after the abandoned attempt. Explain the flow among them, the role of rescanning compound angle-bracket tokens, why JavaScript files bypass the attempt, how a following call, template, operator, or line break affects the decision, and which diagnostic and contextual state must be restored so the speculative attempt does not corrupt subsequent parsing. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Accepting or rolling back an ambiguous generic expression

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. An editor request captures snapshot S, returns deferred work, and later prepares auto-imports from S while an unrelated edit can make snapshot T canonical. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these mandatory roles: (1) the request wrapper that lends a referenced snapshot and language service to a callback and transfers cleanup into returned deferred work; (2) the host-level derivation routine that prepares auto-imports for a document using the supplied base snapshot's filesystem and overlays without adopting the result; (3) the session-level bridge that obtains the derived snapshot's default project, handles its absence, and queues possible background adoption before returning a language service; (4) the mutex-protected adoption routine that accepts or discards the derived snapshot according to whether its base is still current; and (5) final snapshot disposal that releases program-level resources only when no snapshot still owns the program. Explain the causal call and ownership flow with declaration citations and supporting source evidence, distinguishing the request's reference to S, the derived snapshot's initial reference, language-service reachability, and shared-program ownership. Compare adoption before T exists with rejection after T is current; account for a callback error, a callback with no deferred work, deferred work returning a cancellation error, and failure to find a default project in the derived snapshot. Assume returned deferred work is actually invoked. Does canceling the request itself cancel the already-enqueued adoption, and does rejecting adoption invalidate a language service already returned from the derived snapshot? Explain the relevant contexts and resource lifetimes rather than inferring ownership from object reachability. Finally, contrast a discarded snapshot sharing a program with another live snapshot against the last snapshot owning that program, including ordinary parsed files, mapped output bundles, supplemental files, and checker-pool cleanup. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Request snapshot ownership when auto-import preparation loses an adoption race

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. A content mapper returns a canonical virtual document, two supplemental virtual documents, position mappings, and its own diagnostics already located in the original document. Compiler diagnostics can instead refer to copied virtual text, transformed atoms, or entirely synthesized gaps. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these mandatory roles: (1) the protocol-result decoder that assembles canonical and supplemental mapped outputs and converts the mapper's own diagnostic ranges from the negotiated encoding to original-text offsets; (2) the result-to-source-files routine that validates and parses the whole output bundle, attaches external diagnostics to the canonical file, and establishes mapping metadata and supplemental-to-canonical relationships; (3) the language-service collector that gathers the applicable diagnostic categories from the canonical file and every supplemental file; (4) the language-service conversion coordinator that separates entirely synthesized compiler diagnostics into per-source-file aggregates while passing other diagnostics through to LSP conversion; and (5) the general virtual-range mapping primitive used to distinguish exact, atomic, approximate, and unmappable diagnostic spans. Ground the explanation in declaration citations and causal data-flow evidence, including supporting conversion helpers when needed. Compare a valid empty mapping list with a missing in-memory mapping object, and explain why external diagnostics must not be mapped a second time merely because their attached file has a span map. Trace a diagnostic wholly inside copied text, one wholly inside an atom, one wholly inside a gap, and one crossing a copied segment and a gap; explain why approximate mapping is different from having no counterpart. Account for a zero-length diagnostic on a segment boundary, UTF-16 input containing a non-BMP character, an external diagnostic offset inside that character's surrogate pair, and one invalid supplemental output after an otherwise valid canonical result. Explain whether synthesized diagnostics in different supplemental files become one shared aggregate or separate aggregates, what original document URI and fallback ranges related information uses, and what remains visible if the client does not support related diagnostic information. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Preserving diagnostic provenance across canonical and supplemental virtual documents

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. A project has attempted module lookups beneath a missing directory, has cached source and package metadata, and has an open editor overlay. A watcher batch creates a previously missing ancestor directory, reports a cached source as changed without changing its disk bytes, changes tracked package metadata, and deletes a directory containing cached or open files. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these mandatory roles: (1) the session watcher-notification handler that queues recognized events, distinguishes diagnostic-refresh relevance from tracked-config changes, and cancels cache warming; (2) the snapshot change-processing coordinator that chooses excessive-event invalidation or the ordinary filtering, alias-expansion, cache-refresh, and overlay reconciliation pipeline; (3) the filesystem-builder routine that expands directory deletions and filters changed/deleted events while deliberately retaining creations; (4) the project dirty-state routine that differentiates one changed program file from deletion, package metadata changes, multiple changed files, and changes to prior resolution lookups; and (5) the tracked-filesystem predicate that recognizes a seen path or a path beneath a previously missing ancestor directory. Use declaration citations and supporting source evidence to connect event intake, filesystem state, failed-lookup tracking, and the eventual single-file-update eligibility or full-rebuild decision. Compare creating a descendant of a recorded missing directory with creating an unrelated directory; explain how failed directory probes enter the tracking set and why a creation cannot be filtered merely for lacking a source-file extension. Contrast one changed source with a second distinct changed source, a deleted source, and changed package metadata already observed by the project. Explain when an unchanged disk-content notification is eliminated and how open/close overlay reconciliation changes the conclusion. For directory deletion, distinguish cached descendants, open descendants absent from the disk cache, and transient dependency files absent from that cache. Finally, compare an excessive batch entirely outside observed state, one overlapping dependencies only, and one overlapping observed state outside dependencies: specify both the cache invalidation scope and the project dirty-state consequences, including why queued events or scheduled refreshes alone do not prove that a program was rebuilt. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: From watcher batches to missing-lookup invalidation and full project rebuilds

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. A workspace package is reachable through two dependency-directory symlinks to the same realpath. Its exports change while another package remains clean, and a request asks for auto-imports using an existing registry. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these mandatory roles: (1) the registry scheduler that decides full rebuild versus package-granular update, performs parallel discovery and unique-realpath extraction with type-package fallback, and installs successful bucket results; (2) the granular dependency-bucket updater that replaces dirty-package exports and repairs package-file, path, ambient-module, and entrypoint associations; (3) the word-prefix lookup index's filtered-copy routine that compacts retained entries and remaps character posting lists; (4) the language-service gate that checks preparation for the importing file, canonicalizes supplemental files for that check, and refuses an unprepared registry; and (5) the view's common bucket-query routine that excludes self-imports, applies dependency accessibility, and handles nearer-package shadowing while traversing ancestors. Cite declarations and supporting evidence for the causal flow from dirty state to extraction, immutable replacement, readiness checking, and visible candidates. Explain why the two symlinks can share extraction work while still needing separate bucket installations, and distinguish a main package with usable entrypoints from one requiring the corresponding type-package fallback. Compare a known dirty workspace package with an unclassified dependency change, a changed dependency set, and an expanded recursive-directory-traversal requirement; show which force a full rebuild. Explain how old snapshots retain their indexes, why filtering entries without remapping posting lists would corrupt lookups, and how removed package entrypoints are removed from the registry-wide map. Contrast cancellation before a granular updater starts with a successful extraction and installation: determine from actual error checks which old bucket can remain and how the preparation gate reacts, without assuming all canceled operations roll back atomically. Finally, compare no parseable ancestor package metadata with parseable metadata containing no dependencies, a package directly imported despite not being declared there, and a nearer same-named package with no indexed exports; can an outer package supply candidates in the last case? Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Granular export-cache refresh under shared extraction, cancellation, and package shadowing

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. A dynamic content mapper watches a configuration file and has produced a cached canonical-plus-supplemental output bundle. The watched configuration changes while the original source text stays identical, and concurrent project construction can request that same source again. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these mandatory roles: (1) the project-collection helper that decides whether watched paths or a refresh-all request affect a mapper project, refreshes it, and removes single-file-update eligibility; (2) the mapper project lease's refresh routine that closes opened remote project handles under lifecycle/state locks and marks them for reopening; (3) the host routine that lazily opens a remote project, validates dynamic versus static configuration identity and watched-file contracts, and commits successful project metadata; (4) the editor compiler-host routine that obtains a mapped source-file bundle through the identity- and locale-sensitive cache, binds a newly produced bundle, and checks supplemental filename collisions; and (5) the generic reference-counted acquisition routine that serializes production for a cache key, reuses successful values, and removes speculative entries on production failure. Explain the causal call and state flow with declaration citations and supporting identity/key evidence. Compare a watched-path hit, an unrelated path, and refresh-all; include the early exits when no program or watched-file set exists. Does a failed remote close leave the local entry opened, and does the project helper stop invalidation on that error? Contrast reopening with the same configuration identity against reopening with a different identity while source bytes and parse options are unchanged, then change only diagnostic locale. Explain what shares or separates cached bundles and why a static mapper returning a configuration identity or watched files, a dynamic mapper returning an empty identity, and a relative watched filename are rejected. For two concurrent misses for the same cache key, distinguish successful production from a first production failure and explain whether the waiter can observe a cached failed value. Finally, compare a transformation error with a physical-file collision at a compiler-assigned supplemental filename: show where cache acquisition is undone, why collision checking also matters on a cache hit, and why reference ownership is for the output bundle rather than each supplemental file independently. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Dynamic mapper reopening, identity changes, and successful-output bundle ownership

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. An exported declaration's inferred type refers through a chain of initially invisible internal import aliases. Emitting one alias can make another alias necessary. In variants, the referenced type is an inaccessible local name, an unexported name in another external module, or an externally nameable type whose only initially available module spelling traverses a dependency installation directory. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the symbol-to-type-syntax serializer that chooses qualified references versus import-type syntax and handles module-mode and portability fallbacks; (2) the accessibility worker that first delegates accessible-chain discovery and then distinguishes an unnameable external-module symbol from an inaccessible local one; (3) the declaration tracker's symbol-observation entry that requests alias visibility while excluding type parameters and specially watched class self-references; (4) its accessibility-result consumer that queues newly visible aliases or reports a context-dependent diagnostic; and (5) the declaration-transform worklist drain that revisits late-visible declarations and replaces their earlier output forms. Explain the actual callback/call edges among these roles, including intervening adapters, rather than assuming their numbered order is the execution order. Ground the explanation in source evidence for the alias worklist, original-node identity, replacement map, diagnostic context, and import-mode state. Why would draining only the aliases present at the start leave stale declaration output? Distinguish no replacement, deletion, and expansion into several statements. Explain why unresolved names avoid an additional accessibility diagnostic, and when retrying module spelling with a different resolution mode prevents a portability error. Identify the resulting declaration-emit invariants and the limits of the internal-alias behavior shown by this revision. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Declaration serialization through late alias visibility and inaccessible names

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. For an ES2015-targeted async generator, consider a labeled asynchronous iteration loop inside a repeatedly executed outer loop, with delegated yields in its body. Compare normal exhaustion, a labeled break, a user-body exception, a rejected iterator advance, and a cleanup method that itself rejects. Several generators in the same source file request overlapping runtime helpers. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the loop-lowering routine that constructs advancement, user-code tracking, a captured-error record, and nested cleanup/rethrow blocks; (2) the yield visitor that distinguishes ordinary yields from delegation and composes iterator adaptation, delegation, and await markers; (3) the factory routine that constructs the async-generator runtime wrapper call, forwards the receiver and arguments, and marks its inner generator's emit behavior; (4) the emit-context routine that recursively requests helper dependencies and records unique requests; and (5) the printer routine that orders attached helpers and decides whether to write their definitions. Trace AST and helper dataflow across those roles, citing the intervening function-body wrapping and source-file helper attachment where necessary. Explain exactly when cleanup is attempted, which exception survives simultaneous body and cleanup failures, and why the captured error must be reset on a later outer-loop iteration. Contrast an iterator-advance failure with a failure after entry into user code. Explain how labels survive the rewrite and how an await marker differs from a value yielded to the consumer. Show why requesting helpers is insufficient until requests are transferred to an emitted node, and why disabling inline helpers or recording external helpers changes emitted definitions without undoing the transformed calls. Establish whether this revision introduces a switch-based generator state machine or retains an inner generator, using actual source evidence. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Async-generator delegation, iterator cleanup, and emitted helper dependencies

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. A derived class compiled to ES2015 uses standard decorators, a decorated computed-name auto-accessor with a side-effecting name expression, a private instance method called by a field initializer, and a constructor parameter property. Its explicit super call is inside a try block. Decorators register value initializers and extra instance initializers. Compare assignment-style and define-style public fields, then a fieldless variant in which a decorated instance method still registers extra initializers. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the script-target dispatcher whose composed transform definitions establish the decorator-before-field stage order; (2) the decorator-stage property visitor that wraps values, consumes earlier pending initializers, queues this member's extra initializers, and expands decorated auto-accessors; (3) the decorator-stage constructor visitor that drains remaining instance initializers and places them around the discovered super-call path; (4) the field-stage constructor-body builder that orders private-method branding, parameter properties, and ordinary field initialization while preserving the super-call location; and (5) the field-stage property-expression worker that selects private storage, assignment, or property definition and recovers parameter-property values through original-node metadata. Trace the handoff through transformed nodes, initializer queues, generated-name reuse, and emit-context metadata, identifying supporting call edges with source evidence. Explain which initializer runs before which field value, why a member's extra initializers must not run before that member's own initialization, and how the final queue is handled when there is no later field. Show how the computed name is evaluated once despite expansion into several declarations. Explain why private-method branding must precede field initializers and why moving inserted statements outside the super-containing try block changes failure behavior. Analyze the counterfactuals of reversing the transform stages, dropping original-node associations, or overwriting a parameter-property initializer without preserving decorator effects. Limit claims about receiver and exception semantics to what this checkout implements. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Decorator initializer queues crossing the class-field lowering boundary

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. During inference into a homomorphic mapped type, the checker must reconstruct an input type from source property values. Compare a readonly array, a readonly tuple with optional elements, a partially inferable object containing a context-sensitive member, and a source with neither eligible properties nor a string index signature. Now let both the source and mapped template recursively produce newer instantiations sharing recursion identities, and repeat the same source/target/constraint request after the first attempt was suppressed. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the reverse-type constructor that checks source eligibility, eagerly reconstructs arrays and tuples, and leaves ordinary objects as lazy reverse-mapped shells; (2) the reverse-inference coordinator that keys memoization by three type identities, maintains separate source and target stacks, and saves/restores expansion flags; (3) the worker that treats the constraint's indexed access as an inference variable, infers against the mapped template, and widens the result or falls back; (4) the shared deep-nesting classifier that uses recursion identities, intersections, and the ordering of type identities rather than stack length alone; and (5) the mapped-template accessor that lazily adds optionality, instantiates the template with its mapper, and caches it. Explain the call/dataflow edges, including the supporting lazy member-resolution path for object shells. Distinguish both-sided expansion from one-sided expansion and describe exactly what is cached when the worker is skipped. Can the first suppressed attempt and a later cache hit return different representations of failure, and where are those normalized for properties or collection elements? Explain tuple optionality reversal and readonly preservation, why the template must reflect its instantiated mapper, and why restoring stack/flag state prevents one sibling property from inheriting another's expansion state. Analyze the counterfactuals of treating every deep stack as recursion or ignoring the constraint in the cache key. Cite implementation evidence rather than assuming all recursive types are rejected. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Reverse-mapped inference under recursive expansion and cached failure

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Compiler emit records several source locations at the same generated position, sometimes moves backward in the original source, and inserts a generated-only segment between mapped regions. The source includes a non-BMP character, so encoded columns and in-memory text positions need not use the same units. After serialization, a caller builds both directions of a position mapper and queries exact mapping boundaries, gaps, and positions beyond the last mapping. In a variant, a valid mapping prefix is followed by a truncated segment; in another, only a higher-numbered source entry has usable mappings. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the generator's internal accumulator that decides when to commit its pending segment and when to replace or enrich it; (2) the decoder's next-segment routine that tracks delta state, resets generated columns at line boundaries, and detects malformed segment structure; (3) the document-position mapper builder that resolves source paths, converts UTF-16 coordinates through host line information, rejects a failed decode, and constructs sorted/deduplicated indexes; (4) the generated-to-source query that chooses a mapping or refuses an unmapped segment; and (5) the source-to-generated query that canonicalizes a source filename and searches its source bucket. Trace the dataflow across these stages with supporting source evidence for public mapping-update guards and pending-segment serialization. Explain why a generated-only update can invalidate source/name association at a position while a later source update at that position may be ignored. Show which delta fields persist across generated line boundaries and why source backtracking can require another committed segment even without generated movement. Determine the actual binary-search bias in gaps instead of relying on a 'closest' comment, and explain why round trips need not be identity operations. Account for loss of the entire decoded prefix on a later error, missing host line information, duplicate positions, and the actual source-bucket range guard for sparse source indexes. Identify the observed failure/selection behavior without proposing fixes. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Source-map segment accumulation, decode failure, and asymmetric position lookup

"flow": "For an ordinary call to an overloaded generic function, resolveCallExpression (8645) type-checks the callee, takes its apparent type, and reads the call signatures via getSignaturesOfType, then delegates to resolveCall (9028). resolveCall normalizes/orders the candidates with reorderCandidates, computes effective arguments, and because a callback argument is context-sensitive it sets s.argCheckMode = CheckModeSkipContextSensitive (when there is more than one candidate or the lone candidate is generic). It then calls chooseOverload (9213) first under subtypeRelation and again under assignableRelation if needed. chooseOverload walks candidates: it drops those with wrong type-argument or value arity, for generic candidates either validates explicit type arguments (checkTypeArguments) or infers them (inferTypeArguments) and instantiates the signature, and screens each with isSignatureApplicable. Because the callback's parameter/return types depend on the selected overload, the first screening intentionally runs with context-sensitive arguments excluded (CheckModeSkipContextSensitive) so their one-time permanent contextual typing is not prematurely fixed to a parameter type of the wrong overload. When a candidate survives that phase, chooseOverload switches s.argCheckMode back to CheckModeNormal and performs a second round of type-argument inference plus applicability checking for that same candidate, now contextually typing the callback against the candidate's parameters; that is why the candidate is checked again after initially excluding context-sensitive arguments. If a candidate passes the second check it is substituted back into s.candidates and returned. Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. A workspace package is reachable through two dependency-directory symlinks to the same realpath. Its exports change while another package remains clean, and a request asks for auto-imports using an existing registry. After serialization, a caller builds both directions of a position mapper and queries exact mapping boundaries, gaps, and positions beyond the last mapping. In a variant, a valid mapping prefix is followed by a truncated segment; in another, only a higher-numbered source entry has usable mappings. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the generator's internal accumulator that decides when to commit its pending segment and when to replace or enrich it; (2) the decoder's next-segment routine that tracks delta state, resets generated columns at line boundaries, and detects malformed segment structure; (3) the document-position mapper builder that resolves source paths, converts UTF-16 coordinates through host line information, rejects a failed decode, and constructs sorted/deduplicated indexes; (4) the generated-to-source query that chooses a mapping or refuses an unmapped segment; and (5) the source-to-generated query that canonicalizes a source filename and searches its source bucket. Trace the dataflow across these stages with supporting source evidence for public mapping-update guards and pending-segment serialization. Explain why a generated-only update can invalidate source/name association at a position while a later source update at that position may be ignored. Show which delta fields persist across generated line boundaries and why source backtracking can require another committed segment even without generated movement. Determine the actual binary-search bias in gaps instead of relying on a 'closest' comment, and explain why round trips need not be identity operations. Account for loss of the entire decoded prefix on a later error, missing host line information, duplicate positions, and the actual source-bucket range guard for sparse source indexes. (e) If the cleanup method itself rejects while an original body error exists, the inner finally's `if (errorRecord) throw errorRecord.error` runs after the cleanup call, so the original body error survives and the cleanup rejection is replaced; with no prior body error the cleanup rejection propagates. visitYieldExpression (forawait.go:232) distinguishes ordinary yields from delegation: ordinary yields become `yield __await(expr)` (via createDownlevelAwait), while `yield*` becomes `yield __await(__asyncDelegator(__asyncValues(expr)))`. The __await marker differs from a value yielded to the consumer: it is an internal boxing object; the __asyncGenerator step function tests `r.value instanceof __await` and, if so, resolves r.value.v and resumes the generator (fulfill/reject), whereas an unmarked value falls to settle(q[0][2], r) and is delivered as the consumer's {value, done}. The __asyncDelegator verb has the same p = !p alternation between wrapping with __await and forwarding to the consumer. So an await marker stays inside the driver loop, a plain value is handed out.

Helper dataflow: every New*Helper factory calls RequestEmitHelper (emitcontext.go:697), which recurses over Dependencies and records helpers uniquely in the OrderedSet; asyncGeneratorHelper and asyncDelegatorHelper both depend on awaitHelper (helpers.go:293,312). Requesting alone is insufficient because the printer's emitHelpers (printer.go:4635) reads only per-node attachments via GetEmitHelpers(node); the pending set must be drained by ReadEmitHelpers and transferred onto an emitted node. That transfer happens in the source-file visitor, e.g. for the async/for-await transforms at forawait.go:324 (and async.go:54, objectrestspread.go:73, etc.), so the helper definitions are emitted with the source file (or a function body at printer.go:1621). Because several generators in one file request the same helpers, AddEmitHelper uses AppendIfUnique and the OrderedSet dedups, while compareEmitHelpers orders by Priority.

Finally, emitHelpers computes shouldSkip = NoEmitHelpers || HasRecordedExternalHelpers(sourceFile); HasRecordedExternalHelpers is true when the source file's emit node has an externalHelpersModuleName or the EFExternalHelpers flag (emitcontext.go:775). Under --importHelpers the module transform synthesizes a tslib import and flags EFExternalHelpers/externalHelpersModuleName (externalmoduleinfo.go:262-342). In both the noEmitHelpers and importHelpers cases only the inline definition writing is skipped; the transformed call sites were already baked into the tree by the factory routines, so the runtime calls remain and are simply bound to the external module instead of local helper vars."}
